source.title_on_document: Augmenting Minds or Automating Skills? The Differential Role of Human Capital in Generative AI's Impact on Creative Tasks

supplement.where: Online Appendices A to F cited in the text (pp. 17, 19-20, 22-23, 24, 29). The author note (p. 1) says all data, code, output, and materials are at https://osf.io/ynhtu/?view_only=31642f7caac74082940eb1153d4e9e55; the paper does not say the appendices sit there.
supplement.holds: Appendix A: survey measures and rater criteria (Exp. 1); B: song demo materials; C: rater criteria (Exp. 2); D: Exp. 1 supplementary analyses and omnibus model; E: Exp. 2 omnibus model; F: simple-slope figures for usefulness and overall impression. The embedding-similarity analysis for Exp. 1 has no numbers in the main text and may be detailed in Appendix D.

paper_design_summary: Two experiments in China randomly assigned people to write with a GPT-4 chat tool or without AI. In Experiment 1, 162 lab participants wrote one flash fiction (under 500 Chinese characters), and online raters scored novelty, usefulness, and overall enjoyment. In Experiment 2, people recruited online had one week to write song lyrics to an assigned demo; 329 lyrics from 299 participants were rated as text and again as recorded songs, and the paper also reports an embedding-similarity comparison.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of a GPT-4 dialogue tool to write the flash fiction versus writing without AI assistance
assignment.quote: they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: one group used generative AI (GPT-4) to compose a flash-fiction of under 500 Chinese characters, while the other group completed the task without AI assistance.
assignment.locator: p. 16, Experiment 1, Samples and Procedures; Figure 1, p. 48

arms.name: AI group
arms.description: Wrote the flash fiction with a GPT-4 chat interface built on the OpenAI API; received basic fiction-writing instructions plus guidance on prompt crafting.

arms.name: No-AI group
arms.description: Wrote the flash fiction without AI assistance; received basic fiction-writing instructions.

participants.exclusions: None reported for participants. The paper says 162 individuals participated and all regressions in Table 2 have 162 observations. Two raters were excluded for failing attention checks. Arm sizes are not stated; the supplementary t-tests on prompt length among AI users split 111 people (e.g., N_low = 54, N_high = 57, t(109), p. 21), which suggests but does not state an AI arm of 111.
participants.who: People with an interest in story creation recruited through social media and online interest groups: 101 college students and professionals from other sectors; 68.52 percent female; mean age 26.27; 95.06 percent with at least a bachelor's degree. Paid 30 CNY.
participants.quote: 162 individuals participated in the first experiment, each compensated 30 CNY.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, in a dialogue-based interface built by the authors
ai_tool.how_used: Free conversation with the chatbot while composing the story (Figure 3 shows a user asking for story ideas and an expanded concept). The AI group got extra instruction on effective prompt crafting.

task.description: Write one flash fiction of under 500 Chinese characters in the lab, after an IQ test and demographic questionnaire.
task.duration: Single lab session; writing time not stated (the paper says participants worked within a constrained timeframe, p. 22).

outcomes.name: Novelty (rater mean)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual assessment technique; online panel of raters, 10-point scale; novelty = novel and distinctive ideas, originality and uniqueness; ICC2 = .90-.91; average 43.87 raters per story (SD 1.77). OLS with controls for education, IQ, specific human capital, age, gender, openness, AI use frequency, purpose for experiment, mind perception of AI, and the AI identification ratio (share of raters who believed the story used AI, a rater judgment made after treatment). Robust SEs. Omnibus model with all interactions in online Appendix D.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of the GPT-4 dialogue tool to write song lyrics versus writing lyrics without AI support; each participant was also assigned one of ten song demos
assignment.quote: After registration and an online IQ test (Nstart = 685), participants were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted group or a control group that composed lyrics without AI support.
assignment.locator: p. 23, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures; Figure 2, p. 49

arms.name: AI-assisted group
arms.description: Wrote lyrics with the GPT-4 chat interface; basic lyric-writing instructions plus guidance on using generative AI.

arms.name: Control (no AI)
arms.description: Wrote lyrics without AI support; basic lyric-writing instructions.

participants.exclusions: 685 registered and took the IQ test before random assignment (N_start); 611 reached the information session (N_information); 348 submitted lyrics and the follow-up questionnaire (N_submission); dropout in the lyrics-creation stage was 43.04 percent. Of the submissions, 329 works from 299 participants were deemed suitable for song recording by professional producers and singers; 289 of the 299 wrote lyrics for only one song. Attrition by arm is not reported. Regressions use 329 works (Tables 4-8). Arm sizes are not stated; supplementary t-tests among AI users split 197 people (e.g., N_low = 131, N_high = 66, t(195), p. 28), which suggests but does not state an AI arm of 197.
participants.who: Recruited from universities, companies, and online music platforms, with a range of lyric-writing experience (64.44 percent had never published or presented lyrics). Final sample of 299: mean age 24.10, 63.88 percent female, 93.31 percent with a bachelor's degree or higher. Paid 100 CNY plus a professionally recorded song.
participants.quote: Among the submissions, 329 works from 299 participants were deemed suitable for song recording by professional producers and singers.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, in a dialogue-based interface built by the authors (same tool as Experiment 1)
ai_tool.how_used: Free use of the chatbot while writing lyrics at home over one week; the AI group got guidance on using generative AI.

task.description: Write Chinese song lyrics to an assigned demo (accompaniment plus vocal melody sung in 'la-la-la') with a simplified score marking lyric breaks and word counts; participants could also write lyrics for the other nine demos. Lyrics were then sung by trained choir singers and produced into songs.
task.duration: One week, online, at the participant's own pace

outcomes.name: Novelty of lyrics (Novelty_L)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Online panel rated lyric text only, 10-point scale; novelty = originality and unique expression, innovative rhetorical techniques and perspectives; ICC2 = .35-.52; average 5.12 raters per lyric (SD 0.71). OLS with demo fixed effects and controls (education, IQ, specific human capital, age, gender, openness, AI use frequency, purpose, mind perception, AI identification ratio_L). Robust SEs, not clustered by participant.

outcomes.name: Similarity of lyrics (embedding cosine similarity; L2 distance)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Supplementary analysis using 'textual analysis techniques (embedding)'; two variants reported: cosine similarity and L2 distance. Sign reversed relative to diversity: higher cosine similarity and lower L2 distance mean less diversity.

contrasts.reported: Increased similarity among AI-assisted outputs: 'Cosine: b = 0.014, p = .008; L2 distance: b = -0.014, p = .007'. No SE, N, or arm levels printed. Direction recorded for diversity (similarity higher with AI).

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity and L2 distance between text embeddings
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Regression coefficient with p-value; the regression specification and unit are not stated
diversity_detail.notes: Only b and p are printed; statistics_available lists regression_coefficient_se because a coefficient is reported, but no SE is printed. Unit 'output' is a placeholder. Details may be in online Appendix E or the OSF materials.

eligibility.reason: Both experiments randomly assign individuals to a GPT-4 chat tool versus no AI on a creative writing task, with rater-scored novelty and usefulness of the output. Experiment 1 analyzes 162 people in the lab with no reported exclusions; Experiment 2 analyzes 299 people (329 works) after 43 percent dropout and a suitability screen, from 685 who entered assignment. Arm sizes are not stated in either study.

one_line_finding: In Experiment 1 (162 lab participants writing flash fiction), GPT-4 assistance raised rated novelty (b = 0.403, SE 0.19, p = .035) and usefulness (b = 0.352, SE 0.16, p = .032) on a 10-point scale (Table 2, p. 41); in Experiment 2 (299 people, 329 lyrics) the AI effects were not significant (lyrics novelty b = 0.087, SE 0.11; song novelty b = 0.133, p = .061; Tables 4-5, pp. 43-44), and AI-assisted lyrics were more similar (cosine b = 0.014, p = .008; p. 29).
open_questions: Arm sizes are not stated in either experiment. The supplementary t-tests among AI users (111 people in Exp. 1, p. 21; 197 in Exp. 2, p. 28) suggest arm sizes but the paper does not say so.

Every treatment coefficient conditions on the AI identification ratio, the share of raters who believed the output used AI. This is measured after treatment and is strongly related to ratings (e.g., -2.093 for novelty in Table 2), so the coefficients are not unadjusted treatment effects. No unadjusted arm means are printed; only full-sample means and SDs (Tables 1 and 3).

Experiment 2 regressions treat 329 works as independent with robust (not participant-clustered) SEs, although 10 of 299 participants contributed more than one work. Attrition (685 to 348 submissions to 299 analyzed) is not reported by arm.

Is 685 the count randomized? The paper attaches N_start = 685 to registration and the IQ test in the sentence that describes random assignment (p. 23); I recorded it as n_randomized, but it could be read as the count before assignment.

Figure-text inconsistencies: Figure 4 (p. 51) prints p = 0.068 for the low-education slope while the text says p = .968 (p. 19); the text cites Figure 6 for usefulness slopes (0.706, -0.065) but Figure 6 (p. 52) shows novelty slopes (0.605, p = .012; 0.166, p = .514); the text cites Figure 7 for b = 0.389 (lyrics novelty) but Figure 7 (p. 53) plots Novelty_Song with slopes 0.241 and 0.033.
Experiment 1 embedding-similarity result has no numbers or method in the main text (p. 21).
notes: Outcomes left out because they are self-reported: psychological ownership (Exp. 1 b = -1.239, p = .001; Exp. 2 b = -1.124) and creative self-efficacy (Exp. 2 b = 0.284, p = .014), pp. 21 and 29. Process measures (prompt length, interaction rounds) are not output scores and are not listed. The paper's focus is moderation by education, IQ, and specific human capital; interaction coefficients are recorded inside each outcome's 'reported' field. 'Overall impression' outcomes are coded construct 'other' because they rate enjoyment, quality, or liking rather than creativity. PDF page numbers equal the printed page numbers. A raw t(308) df appears for Exp. 2 simple slopes with 329 observations.
